summary:
CosmoPulse is an offline-first health dashboard that helps astronauts assess their own condition on long missions, when Earth is up to 20 minutes away and no clinic is available. It is built around NASA's five human spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments.
The app tracks nine indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen, sleep, mood, body mass, exercise, and radiation dose. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's personal baseline, not just general ranges, and shown as a green, yellow, or red status with plain-language guidance on what to do and when to contact flight surgeons.
Key features include a color-coded dashboard, a clickable body map, trend charts with dashed baselines, a wellbeing check-in with guided breathing, an alert history, and a printable report for ground support. It also flags combined changes, such as poor sleep, low mood, and reduced exercise together.
CosmoPulse is a decision-support prototype using manual and simulated data. It never diagnoses and always points to mission medical protocols.
details:
Project details: CosmoPulse

What it does and how it works

CosmoPulse is an offline-first health dashboard that lets astronauts check their own health during long missions, when a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way. The astronaut logs in, sets personal baselines in a profile, and records readings for nine indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood oxygen (SpO₂), sleep, mood, body mass, exercise, and radiation dose.

For each reading, the app:

  1. Compares it with the astronaut's own baseline using a deviation formula, D = (|X − B| ÷ |B|) × 100.
  2. Checks the trend over recent days and looks for combined changes, such as poor sleep, low mood, and less exercise together.
  3. Shows a green (normal), yellow (attention), or red (urgent) status.
  4. Gives plain-language advice on what to do now and when to contact flight surgeons.

The app has eight tabs: Dashboard, Body Map, Measure, Analytics, Wellbeing, Alerts, Report, and Profile. The Report tab produces a printable summary for ground support.

Benefits

  • Early warning: many spaceflight changes are silent, and trends catch slow drift before it becomes serious.
  • Personal: a very fit astronaut's normal differs from the average adult's, so alerts use personal baselines.
  • Clear for non-experts: each result is explained, with no medical training needed.
  • Autonomy: it works offline and always shows a path to ground support.
  • Mental health: it covers mood, stress, and sleep, which are major risks from isolation and confinement.

Intended impact

The goal is to help crews catch problems early, act on them confidently, and send ground teams clear, structured information despite communication delays. Over time it could support safer Moon and Mars missions by turning health monitoring into a daily routine instead of an emergency response.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Prototype: the screenshots show a browser-based web app, which would typically use HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with SVG for the body map and line charts.
  • Data: manually entered and simulated readings, so no real sensors were needed for the demo.
  • Documentation and presentation: the challenge guide (a Claude Doc) and the 7-slide deck (PowerPoint) were created with Claude.
  • Intended hardware for a real mission: a wrist wearable, automatic blood pressure cuff, infrared thermometer, pulse oximeter, space-rated mass device, personal dosimeter, cabin CO₂ sensors, and a tablet or ruggedized laptop.

Creativity

  • A clickable body map where brain, heart, lungs, bones, muscles, and whole body each show their own indicators and status.
  • A space-themed interface with color-coded cards and sparklines against dashed personal baselines.
  • Combined-signal alerts that treat sleep, mood, and exercise together.
  • A guided breathing exercise built into the wellbeing tab.
  • A supportive tone that avoids pressuring astronauts, since pressure could lead them to hide symptoms.

Factors the team considered

  • Science: each indicator is tied to one of NASA's five hazards, and the ranges follow general adult guidelines.
  • Safety: the app supports decisions and never diagnoses. Its rules are illustrative and must be validated against approved mission medical protocols.
  • Usability: simple instructions, plain language, and large touch-friendly controls suited to gloves and low gravity.
  • Reliability: offline operation, input validation, and backups.
  • Privacy: health data belongs to the astronaut, and sharing is an explicit choice.
  • Environment: future modes for spacecraft, station, Moon, and Mars, since each has different gravity, radiation, and isolation challenges.
dataRefs: NASA Human Research Program: Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
